did_you_know.text: Did you know? Amos’s prophecy against Moab opens with the formula “For three transgressions... and for four,” emphasizing the accumulation of serious sins. The specific sin mentioned here is burning the bones of the king of Edom and reducing them to lime.

Did you know? Moab’s punishment is described through fire, the noise of battle, the blast of a trumpet, and the destruction of the palaces of Kerioth. The description portrays a national defeat and the overthrow of its rule.

Did you know? Judah is also included in Amos’s prophecies of judgment. The sin mentioned is rejecting the LORD’s law and failing to keep his statutes, as well as following the falsehoods in which their ancestors had walked.

Did you know? Amos describes social injustice with the words, “They sell the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals”—a picture of trafficking in people or perverting justice for a tiny profit.

Did you know? The prophet accuses those in power of trampling on the poor and turning the humble aside from their way. The same verse also mentions profaning the holiness of the LORD’s name through sexually immoral behavior.

Did you know? The garments mentioned in the verse are clothes taken as pledges, and the wine is connected with penalties or fines. Amos portrays a situation in which the property of the powerless is used by those in power, even in a religious setting.

Did you know? The LORD reminds Israel of the destruction of the Amorites, whose height is compared to the height of cedars and whose strength is compared to that of oaks. The image emphasizes that even a very powerful enemy cannot stand before the LORD.

Did you know? The exodus from Egypt and the forty years of traveling in the wilderness are presented here as acts of the LORD’s kindness toward Israel and as preparation for inheriting the land of the Amorites.

Did you know? According to the verse, the LORD raised up both prophets and Nazirites from among the Israelites. In this way, prophecy and the Nazirite calling are presented as gifts or missions given from within the people themselves.

Did you know? Israel’s response to the LORD’s messengers is described as giving the Nazirites wine to drink and commanding the prophets not to prophesy. This highlights not only moral sin but also the active rejection of the LORD’s messages.
